actual_step_source.1.1: 1.1 Fix $\theta$. Since $P_\theta$ is a probability measure, the constant $1$ has $L^2(P_\theta)$ norm $1$. Applying [F4] to $T$ and $1$ gives $\mathbb E_\theta|T|\leq(\mathbb E_\theta[T^2])^{1/2}<\infty$. Put $\mu=\mathbb E_\theta[T]$ and $b=\mu-\psi(\theta)$. Then [F1] gives $b=\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(T)$ and $T-\psi(\theta)=(T-\mu)+b$. [given, F1, F4]
actual_step_source.2.1: 2.1 Since $T,\mu\in L^1(P_\theta)$ by step 1.1 and $P_\theta(\mathcal X)=1$, [F3] gives $\mathbb E_\theta[T-\mu]=\mathbb E_\theta[T]-\mu\mathbb E_\theta[1]=0$. For every finite $c$, $(T-c)^2\leq2T^2+2c^2$, so the centered square and squared error are integrable. Expanding $(T-\psi(\theta))^2=((T-\mu)+b)^2$ now gives $\operatorname{MSE}_\theta(T)=\mathbb E_\theta[(T-\mu)^2]+b^2=\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)+\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(T)^2$ by [F1] and [F2]. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra] ∎

actual_step_source.1.1: 1.1 Write $u$ for the measurable function defining $U$. For each $\theta$, $P_\theta^S$ is a probability measure: preimages under the measurable map $S$ preserve the empty set, disjoint countable unions, and the whole space. By [L1], $K$ is a parameter-independent probability kernel from the statistic space to the data space, so it is a randomized procedure for the pushforward experiment by [F15]. Thus [F2] and [F3] show that $h_+(s)=\int u^+dK(s,\cdot)$, $h_-(s)=\int u^-dK(s,\cdot)$, and $r(s)=\int|u|dK(s,\cdot)$ are Borel. Let $g=h_+-h_-$ where $r<\infty$ and $g=0$ elsewhere; [F6] makes both terms finite on this Borel set, and [F3] makes $g$ Borel. [given, L1, F2, F3, F6, F15, construct]
actual_step_source.2.1: 2.1 Fix $\theta$ and a Borel statistic event $B$. For nonnegative simple functions of the data, [L1] and finite linearity give $\int_B\int s(x)K(t,dx)P_\theta^S(dt)=\mathbb E_\theta[\mathbf1_{\{S\in B\}}s(X)]$. Approximate $u^+$ and $u^-$ increasingly by simple functions using [F4]; [F5] passes each equality to the limit. Applying the same identity to $|u|$ with $B=\mathsf S$ gives $\mathbb E_\theta r(S)=\mathbb E_\theta|U|<\infty$. If $N=\{r(S)=+\infty\}$ had positive probability, then $m\mathbf1_N\leq r(S)$ for every positive integer $m$, so [F6] would give $mP_\theta(N)\leq\mathbb E_\theta r(S)$ for all $m$, a contradiction; thus $r(S)<\infty$ almost surely. By [F6], $h_+(S),h_-(S)\leq r(S)$, so $|g(S)|\leq2r(S)$ and $g(S)$ is integrable. The two finite event-integral identities may therefore be subtracted, giving $\mathbb E_\theta[\mathbf1_{\{S\in B\}}g(S)]=\mathbb E_\theta[\mathbf1_{\{S\in B\}}U]$. By [F7], [F8], and [F9], $g(S)$ is a version of $\mathbb E_\theta[U\mid\sigma(S)]$ as an almost-sure class for every $\theta$. [given, L1, F1, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, F13, step 1.1]
actual_step_source.3.1: 3.1 By [F10], $g(S)$ is square-integrable under each $P_\theta$. By [F11], $\mathbb E_\theta[g(S)]=\mathbb E_\theta[U]=\psi(\theta)$; hence it is an unbiased finite-variance estimator. [F1, F10, F11, F13, step 2.1]
actual_step_source.4.1: 4.1 Fix $\theta$. The residual $U-g(S)$ is orthogonal in $L^2(P_\theta)$ to every square-integrable $\sigma(S)$-measurable function by [F12]. By step 3.1 and $\psi(\theta)\in\mathbb R$, $g(S)-\psi(\theta)$ is such a function. Expanding the centered square gives $\operatorname{Var}_\theta(U)=\mathbb E_\theta[(U-g(S))^2]+\operatorname{Var}_\theta(g(S))$. The first term is nonnegative, proving the variance inequality. [F1, F12, F13, step 3.1, algebra]
actual_step_source.5.1: 5.1 By [F14], equality in step 4.1 holds exactly when $U=g(S)$ $P_\theta$-almost surely. Since $g(S)$ is $\sigma(S)$-measurable, this is precisely almost-sure $\sigma(S)$-measurability: if $U$ has such a representative, its $L^2$ class lies in the projection subspace and [F12] fixes it. [step 4.1, F12, F14] ∎

relevant_facts.F1: [F1] A finite-variance unbiased estimator is integrable, has expectation $\psi(\theta)$ at every parameter, and has the variance convention stated in the UMVU definition. ([[def-unbiased-estimator-and-umvu]])
relevant_facts.F2: [F2] For a probability kernel, integrating a nonnegative measurable function gives a measurable function of the input, with the corresponding iterated-integral identity. ([[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]])
relevant_facts.F4: [F4] Nonnegative measurable functions admit increasing simple approximations. ([[thm-increasing-simple-approximation-of-a-nonnegative-measurable-function]])
relevant_facts.F7: [F7] Every event in $\sigma(S)$ is $S^{-1}(B)$ for a Borel statistic-space event $B$. ([[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]])
relevant_facts.F9: [F9] Under AC, versions with the same event integrals determine one almost-sure class. ([[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]])

actual_step_source.1.1: 1.1 For $s\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$ let $F_s=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_i x_i=s\}$; it has $\binom ns\geq1$ elements. Define $K(s,A)=|A\cap F_s|/\binom ns$ for every data event $A$. Each section is the uniform probability measure on $F_s$, and every event evaluation is measurable because the statistic space is finite and discrete; thus $K$ is a probability kernel independent of $p$. By [F4], independence makes the joint law the product of the Bernoulli coordinate masses. For $0<p<1$, each vector in $F_s$ has mass $p^s(1-p)^{n-s}$ and $P_p(S=s)>0$, so $K(s,\cdot)$ is the conditional law given $S=s$. At $p=0$ or $p=1$, only $s=0$ or $s=n$ is supported, respectively, and that fiber is a singleton on which the same kernel is the conditional law. Hence $K$ is a common regular conditional law and proves sufficiency by [L1]. [given, F4, L1, construct]
actual_step_source.2.1: 2.1 For $0<p<1$, the uniform fiber law is invariant under coordinate permutations, so the $n$ conditional means $\mathbb E_p[X_i\mid S=s]$ agree. Their sum is $s$, hence each is $s/n$. At $p=0,1$, $X_1=S/n$ almost surely, so the same formula holds on the support. Since $0\leq X_1\leq1$, $U=X_1$ is square-integrable; its Bernoulli law gives $\mathbb E_pX_1=p\cdot1+(1-p)\cdot0=p$ by [F4]. Both spaces are standard Borel by [F5] and $S$ is sufficient by step 1.1, so [F2] and [F1] identify $S/n$ as the Rao–Blackwellized unbiased estimator; [F3] records its conditional-expectation class convention. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

relevant_facts.F1: [F1] Rao–Blackwellization of an unbiased finite-variance estimator is its conditional expectation given a sufficient statistic. ([[thm-rao-blackwell]])
relevant_facts.F2: [F2] $X_1$ is a measurable estimator of $p$, and it is unbiased when its expectation is $p$. ([[def-statistic-and-estimator]], [[def-unbiased-estimator-and-umvu]])
relevant_facts.F4: [F4] A Bernoulli$(p)$ variable takes values $1$ and $0$ with probabilities $p$ and $1-p$, and mutual independence of finite-valued variables means their joint cell probabilities factor. ([[def-bernoulli-and-binomial-random-variables]], [[def-independence-of-finite-random-variables]])

actual_step_source.1.1: 1.1 Let $X$ be any measurable real random variable. For $a<0$, $\{e^{\lambda X}>a\}$ is the whole probability space by [F6]. For $a\ge0$ and $\lambda=0$, this set is the whole space if $a<1$ and empty if $a\ge1$. For $a\ge0$ and $\lambda\ne0$, it is the whole space when $a=0$; when $a>0$, strict increase of the exponential and the inverse relation with $\log$ give $$\{e^{\lambda X}>a\}=\begin{cases}\{X>(\log a)/\lambda\},&\lambda>0,\\\{X<(\log a)/\lambda\},&\lambda<0.\end{cases}$$ Every set on the right is measurable by [F7]. Thus $e^{\lambda X}$ is measurable by the threshold characterization, with no appeal to a continuous-map Borel measurability result qualified by Countable Choice. [F6, F7, given, algebra]
actual_step_source.2.1:
2.1 Let $A:=\{|Y|\le1\}$, measurable by [F9], so $P(A)=1$. Define $
u(B):=\int_B|Y|\,dP$; by [F9] this is a measure. Since $|Y|\mathbf1_A\le\mathbf1_A$, [F9] gives $
u(A)\le P(A)=1$, while $P(A^c)=0$ gives $
u(A^c)=0$. Therefore $\mathbb E|Y|=
u(\Omega)=
u(A)+
u(A^c)\le1$, so $Y$ is integrable by [F9]. Put $p:=\mathbb EY$; then [F1] gives $p\in[0,1]$. The shifted variable $Y-p$ is measurable because $\{Y-p>a\}=\{Y>a+p\}$ for every real $a$. Applying step 1.1 to $X=Y$ and $X=Y-p$ establishes measurability of both exponentials. Applying [F2] with endpoints $0,\lambda$ gives $e^{\lambda y}\le1-y+ye^\lambda$ for every $y\in[0,1]$; taking expectations yields $\mathbb E e^{\lambda Y}\le1-p+pe^\lambda$. [F1, F2, F9, step 1.1, given]
actual_step_source.3.1: 3.1 Define $g(\lambda):=1-p+pe^\lambda>0$ and $\psi(\lambda):=\log g(\lambda)-p\lambda$. Positivity follows from [F6] and $p\in[0,1]$. With $q(\lambda):=pe^\lambda/g(\lambda)\in[0,1]$, [F3]–[F4] give $\psi(0)=\psi'(0)=0$ and $\psi''(\lambda)=q(\lambda)(1-q(\lambda))\in[0,1/4]$. The formula also covers $p=0$ or $p=1$, since then $g$ remains positive. [given, F3, F4, F6, step 2.1, algebra]
actual_step_source.4.1: 4.1 The function $\psi''$ in step 3.1 is continuous. For $\lambda\ge0$, integrating twice by [F5] gives $\psi(\lambda)=\int_0^\lambda(\lambda-s)\psi''(s)\,ds\le\lambda^2/8$. For $\lambda<0$, the same endpoint formula written from $\lambda$ to $0$ gives $\psi(\lambda)=\int_\lambda^0(s-\lambda)\psi''(s)\,ds\le\lambda^2/8$. [F5, step 3.1, algebra]
actual_step_source.5.1: 5.1 By step 2.1 and the exponential addition formula [F8], $\mathbb E e^{\lambda(Y-p)}=e^{-\lambda p}\mathbb E e^{\lambda Y}\le e^{-\lambda p}g(\lambda)=e^{\psi(\lambda)}$; step 4.1 bounds this by $e^{\lambda^2/8}$. This proves the claim for every real $\lambda$, including $\lambda=0$. [F8, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

relevant_facts.F1: [F1] If $X\le W$ almost surely for integrable real variables, then $\mathbb EX\le\mathbb EW$ ([[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]]).
relevant_facts.F4: [F4] Sums, scalar multiples, products, quotients with nonzero denominator, and compositions obey the usual derivative and continuity rules ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule]], [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]).
relevant_facts.F7: [F7] A real-valued function is measurable when all strict upper or all strict lower threshold sets are measurable; the exponential is strictly increasing, positive, and inverse to the natural logarithm on positive inputs ([[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]], [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[def-natural-logarithm]]).
relevant_facts.F9: [F9] Absolute values of measurable real functions are measurable. A statement holding almost surely has a measurable null exceptional set. The probability measure satisfies $P(\Omega)=1$. For nonnegative measurable $g$, the set function $B\mapsto\int_B g\,dP$ is a measure; the nonnegative integral is monotone under pointwise order, indicators integrate to their measures, and integrals over null sets vanish. A real measurable function is integrable exactly when its absolute-value integral is finite ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]], [[def-probability-measure]], [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]], [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]).

actual_step_source.1.1: 1.1 By [F1], $\Omega$ is uncountable. The empty set is at most countable, and complementation exchanges the countable and cocountable alternatives, so $\mathcal A$ contains the empty set and is complement-closed. For a sequence $(A_n)$ in $\mathcal A$, if every $A_n$ is countable then [A1] makes their union countable; otherwise some $A_j$ is cocountable, and $\Omega\setminus\bigcup_n A_n\subseteq\Omega\setminus A_j$ is countable by [F2]. Thus the union lies in $\mathcal A$ in either case, proving all sigma-algebra axioms in [F5]. The assignment $P$ is well-defined: a set and its complement cannot both be countable, since their union would make $\Omega$ countable. [A1, F1, F2, F5, given]
actual_step_source.2.1: 2.1 Let $(A_n)$ be pairwise disjoint members of $\mathcal A$. If every $A_n$ is countable, [A1] makes their union countable; then $P(\bigcup_nA_n)=0=\sum_nP(A_n)$. Otherwise choose $j$ with $A_j$ cocountable. For $n\ne j$, disjointness gives $A_n\subseteq\Omega\setminus A_j$, a countable set, so [F2] makes $A_n$ countable. The union is cocountable and its measure is $1=P(A_j)+\sum_{n\ne j}P(A_n)$. Also $P(\Omega)=1$ and $P$ is nonnegative, so [F3] shows that $P$ is a probability measure. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, given, choose]
actual_step_source.3.1: 3.1 Regard $(\Omega,\mathcal A,P)$ as the observation space and let $Z$ be its identity random element, which has law $P$. For each $t\in U$, the singleton $\{t\}$ is in $\mathcal A$ by [F2], so $f_t=\mathbf1_{\{t\}}$ is measurable and $Pf_t=P(\{t\})=0$. If $s\ne t$, then $f_s(s)=1$ and $f_t(s)=0$, so $t\mapsto f_t$ is injective; since $U$ is uncountable by [F1], $\mathcal F$ is uncountable. [F1, F2, F3, F4, given, step 2.1]
actual_step_source.4.1: 4.1 For any $\omega\in\Omega$, if $\omega\in U$ then the index $t=\omega$ gives $f_t(\omega)=1$, while if $\omega\notin U$ every $t\in U$ differs from $\omega$ and all the function values are zero. Hence the displayed supremum equals $\mathbf1_U(\omega)$. Both $U$ and $\Omega\setminus U$ contain a nondegenerate interval and are uncountable by [F1]; therefore $U\notin\mathcal A$, so the supremum is nonmeasurable. [F1, step 3.1, given] ∎

relevant_facts.F1: [F1] Every nondegenerate real interval is uncountable ([[cor-interval-uncountable]]).
relevant_facts.F2: [F2] Every singleton is countable and every subset of a countable set is countable ([[def-countable]], [[lem-subset-of-countable]]).
relevant_facts.F4: [F4] For one observation, the empirical average is $P_1f=f(Z)$ and $Pf$ is the integral of $f$ ([[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]]).

operations.subject: thm-bias-variance-decomposition

expected_complete_row.quote:
Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

operations.subject: thm-rao-blackwell

expected_complete_row.quote:
Let $T$ be an estimator of a real estimand $\psi$ in a statistical experiment.
It is **unbiased** if it is integrable under every $P_\theta$ and
$$\mathbb E_\theta[T]=\psi(\theta)\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta.$$
Equivalently, its bias from [[def-bias-and-mean-squared-error]] is zero at every
parameter. It is a **finite-variance unbiased estimator** if it is unbiased
and square-integrable under every $P_\theta$.

A finite-variance unbiased estimator $T$ is **uniformly minimum-variance
unbiased** (UMVU) for $\psi$ if, for every $\theta\in\Theta$ and every other
finite-variance unbiased estimator $U$ of the same estimand,
$$\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)\leq\operatorname{Var}_\theta(U).$$
The same estimator must satisfy these inequalities throughout the parameter
space; the definition asserts no existence of a UMVU estimator. Variance has
the meaning in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]].

For $n\in\mathbb N$, a **binomial$(n,p)$ random variable** is a sum $X=\sum_{i<n}X_i$ of $n$ mutually independent Bernoulli$(p)$ variables. When $n=0$, this is the constant zero random variable.

expected_complete_row.quote:
A finite family of finite-valued random variables $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **mutually independent** when for every nonempty $J\subseteq I$ and every selection $x_j\in X_j(\Omega)$,
$$\mathbb P(X_j=x_j\text{ for every }j\in J)=\prod_{j\in J}\mathbb P(X_j=x_j).$$
It is **pairwise independent** when this identity is required only for two distinct indices. The empty family is mutually independent vacuously, and a one-member family is mutually independent.

2. the open interval $(a,b) = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : a < x < b \,\}$

are uncountable ([[def-countable]]).

**What this adds to [[thm-r-uncountable]], and what it does not inherit from it.**
That theorem states exactly one thing: $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable. Its statement
says nothing about any interval, so the present result cannot be read off it. Its
*proof*, on the other hand, is general in every part but its seed: the trisection
rule of its step 2.1 is constructed there for an arbitrary $(a,b) \in I$, and its
steps 4.1, 5.1 and 6.1, together with the interval reasoning of its step 7.1, use
nothing about the starting interval beyond the nesting and the strictness

and to $(0,1)$: the surjection of its step 1.1 is onto $\mathbb{R}$, the recursion
of its step 3.1 is seeded at $(0,(0,1))$, and the conclusion drawn in its step 7.1
is about $\mathbb{R}$. So the construction is re-run below, seeded
instead at the **middle third** of $(a,b)$, against a surjection onto $(a,b)$; the
remarks record why that seed and not $(a,b)$ itself.
